unit.title: Perform manual heating and thermal cutting

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A job needs parts cut from 6 mm stainless steel sheet and from 50 mm mild steel plate. Which choice of process is best?
options: Oxy-fuel for both, with a bigger nozzle for the stainless
Plasma for the thick steel, oxy-fuel for the stainless
Plasma for the stainless, oxy-fuel for the thick steel
Oxy-fuel for both, with extra preheat on the stainless

questions.stem: Why are parts 'nested' (laid out close together) when a plate is marked out for cutting?
options: To use the plate well and cut down waste
So the parts heat each other and cut faster
So that no kerf allowance is needed
To stop the plate from moving on the table

questions.stem: Six strips, each 100 mm wide, are cut from the edge of a wide plate. Each strip needs one cut, and the kerf is about 3 mm. How much plate width is used?
options: 600 mm
615 mm
603 mm
618 mm

questions.stem: Why is the cutting order planned when many parts are cut from one plate?
options: So that the gas cylinders empty evenly
To keep the plate stiff and control distortion
So that every cut can start at the same corner
So that the nozzle never needs cleaning

questions.stem: Which method helps stop a long, narrow strip from bowing as it is flame cut?
options: Cut one edge fully, let it cool, then cut the other edge
Cut both edges at the same time with two torches
Use a much bigger nozzle so the cut is quicker
Quench each strip in water as soon as it is free

questions.stem: Which of these must a hot work permit for cutting on a site normally include?
options: Only the name of the person who does the cutting
The price of the gas used for the job
The make and colour of the cutting torch
The area, the fire precautions and the fire watch

questions.stem: Why must oxygen never be used to 'freshen the air' in a tank or confined space where people are working?
options: Oxygen-rich air makes clothes and hair burn fiercely
Oxygen cools the air too much for people to work
Oxygen turns the steel walls of the tank brittle
Oxygen costs much more than compressed air does

questions.stem: Old steel to be cut has a thick coat of old paint that may contain lead. What should be done before cutting?
options: Cut it as it is, but work quickly to cut down the fumes
Wet the paint with water so it does not burn
Test or strip the paint back from the cut line first
Paint over it with new paint to seal in the lead

questions.stem: Why should gas hoses not be left inside a tank or confined space during a break?
options: The hoses may get too hot from the tank walls
A leak could fill the space with gas or oxygen
The hoses will be harder to coil up at the end of the day
Other workers may trip over them in the dark

questions.stem: Plasma cutting stainless steel gives off fumes that contain chromium compounds. Which control is most suitable?
options: Fume extraction at the cut, and a respirator if needed
A large fan behind the operator, blowing the fumes away
Cutting faster so that less fume is made
No control is needed, as stainless does not rust

questions.stem: A hot work area has been cleared for 10 m, but there is an open floor drain nearby. What is the risk?
options: The drain will block with slag and flood the shop
Water from the drain will put out the torch flame
There is no risk, as drains are below the floor
Sparks can fall in and light gas or waste below

questions.stem: During a fire watch after cutting, what should the fire watcher do?
options: Leave as soon as the torch is out, as the risk is then over
Stay at the gas trolley in case a hose leaks
Watch the whole area, including below and behind walls
Spray the area with oxygen to cool it down

questions.stem: An oxygen cylinder reads 200 bar when full and then holds about 7 000 L. About how much oxygen is left when the gauge reads 50 bar?
options: About 1 750 L
About 5 250 L
About 3 500 L
About 700 L

questions.stem: Why can the contents of an LPG (propane) cylinder not be judged from a pressure gauge?
options: The gauge works only when the cylinder is lying on its side
It is held as a liquid, so the pressure barely changes
LPG has no pressure until the torch is lit
The pressure rises as the cylinder empties

questions.stem: Propane is to be used in place of acetylene for cutting. What must be changed?
options: Nothing at all: the same nozzle and settings work for both
Only the colour of the fuel hose
The oxygen hose, as propane needs a smaller one
The regulator and nozzle, to ones made for propane

questions.stem: Compared with acetylene, what is one advantage of propane as the fuel gas for cutting thick steel?
options: It gives a hotter flame, so piercing is much faster
It needs less oxygen for the preheat flame
It is cheaper, and suits long cuts in thick plate
It needs no flashback arrestors on the set

questions.stem: When several oxygen and fuel gas cylinders are stored, how should they be kept?
options: Upright and secured, with oxygen kept apart from fuel gas
Lying down together in one locked cage
Out in the sun, so that the gas stays warm and flows freely
Next to the cutting bay, so that they are close at hand

questions.stem: Why must the seat of a cutting nozzle be checked before it is fitted to the torch?
options: A dirty seat changes the colour of the flame
A damaged seat makes the nozzle cut too wide
The seat sets the oxygen pressure for the cut
A damaged seat can leak gas and start a fire

questions.stem: A hose has a small burn mark, and its outer cover is damaged. What should be done?
options: Wrap the mark with tape and carry on with the job
Take it out of use and fit a new hose assembly
Turn the pressure down a little and keep working
Turn the hose round so the mark faces the floor

questions.stem: Why are flashback arrestors and hose check valves tested or replaced at set times?
options: Their colour fades in the sun and must match
They slowly change the flame from neutral to oxidising
They can wear or clog and then fail without warning
They are only needed for the first year of use

questions.stem: After a flashback has happened, what must be done before the set is used again?
options: Have the torch and arrestors checked or replaced
Relight the torch at once to check that it works
Open the cylinder valves fully to blow it clear
Change the fuel hose colour to show it has failed

questions.stem: Why is thick or high-carbon steel preheated before it is flame cut?
options: To make the cut edges brighter and smoother
To slow the cooling, so the edges do not crack
To burn off the mill scale so no oxygen is needed
To soften the steel so that it can be cut with a saw

questions.stem: Which is the most reliable way for a supervisor to check that a part has reached the preheat temperature set in a procedure?
options: Spit on the part and listen to the sound
Look at the colour of the steel in the daylight outside
Hold a hand close to it and judge the heat
Use a temperature crayon or a contact thermometer

questions.stem: Where should the preheat temperature be measured on a thick plate that is about to be welded?
options: A set distance back from the joint, as the procedure says
Only in the flame itself, right next to the nozzle tip
On the far end of the plate, away from the joint
In the joint itself, while the flame is still on it

questions.stem: A steel pulley is stuck on its shaft. Why is the pulley heated quickly, rather than heating both parts slowly?
options: So the shaft melts and the pulley can be saved
So that the steel turns soft enough to bend
So the pulley grows before the heat reaches the shaft
So that the paint burns off and acts as a lubricant

questions.stem: What can happen if a part is heated too hot for too long during manual heating?
options: The metal becomes harder and much stronger
The scale protects it, so there is no harm
The part keeps growing in size after it cools
Grain growth can weaken it, and it may distort

questions.stem: Why is a V heat taken only about two-thirds of the way across a bar, and not the full width?
options: Heating the full width would melt or burn the far edge
The cool part acts as a hinge, so the bar bends back
The far edge is always too thin to be heated
So that less gas is used on every heat

questions.stem: Why should water not be sprayed on a red-hot area of high-strength steel during flame straightening?
options: Quick cooling can make it hard and brittle
The water will make the steel expand again
The steam will bend the bar the wrong way
The water stops the heat spot from shrinking

questions.stem: A thin steel panel has a bulge (buckle) in the middle. Which heating pattern is usually used to pull it flat?
options: One long line heat right across the full width
A large V heat from one edge to the centre
Small spot heats on the bulge, one at a time
Heating the whole panel red hot all at once

questions.stem: Oxy-fuel cutting works on mild steel because of two facts about steel and its oxide. Which is one of them?
options: The oxide melts at a higher heat than the steel
The oxide melts at a lower heat than the steel
Steel does not burn in pure oxygen at any heat
The steel melts before it reaches its burning heat

questions.stem: Why can a normal oxy-fuel torch not cut cast iron well?
options: Cast iron is too soft for the oxygen jet
Cast iron has no carbon in it at all
Cast iron melts at a much higher heat than steel
Its high carbon makes it melt before it can burn

questions.stem: Why is a guide or roller attachment used for long straight cuts?
options: It keeps the nozzle height and angle steady
It lets the torch cut with no preheat flame
It stops the sparks from landing on the floor
It makes the kerf wider so slag can escape

questions.stem: Which change is usually made when moving from cutting 10 mm plate to cutting 40 mm plate?
options: Keep the same nozzle but travel twice as fast
Use a smaller nozzle and less cutting oxygen
Use a larger nozzle and slow the travel speed
Turn off the preheat once the cut has started

questions.stem: A 1.2 m cut is made at a travel speed of 400 mm per minute. How long does the cut take?
options: 2 minutes
3 minutes
4 minutes
30 seconds

questions.stem: Heavy slag sticks hard to the bottom edge of a cut in 12 mm plate. Which is a likely cause?
options: The plate was cleaned too well before cutting
The nozzle was held too close to clean plate
The cutting oxygen was the right pressure
Travel too slow, or cutting oxygen too low

questions.stem: The cut face is hollowed out (concave) from top to bottom. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cutting oxygen pressure too high
Preheat flame set much too small
Plate too thin for the nozzle
Travel speed a little too slow for it

questions.stem: A cut edge is not square: it slopes the same way along its full length. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cutting oxygen pressure set too low
Plate surface dirty with mill scale
Torch not held square to the plate
Travel speed changed during the cut

questions.stem: A drawing allows ±1.5 mm on a flame-cut part 300 mm long. Which measured length is acceptable?
A flame-cut edge on high-carbon steel is hard and has small cracks. What should be done before it is welded or bent?
options: Paint it to seal the cracks and weld over them
Weld over it quickly so the cracks melt away
Bend it cold first to open the cracks up
Grind off the hard layer and preheat next time

questions.stem: How does a plasma cutter cut metal?
options: A very hot arc in ionised gas melts and blows it out
An oxygen jet burns the steel as in oxy-fuel cutting
A spinning abrasive disc grinds through the metal
A flame of compressed air and fuel gas melts it

questions.stem: Why must the compressed air for a plasma cutter be clean and dry?
options: Wet air makes the cut much colder and quieter
Dry air is needed so that the machine can be earthed
Water and oil wear the consumables and spoil the cut
Clean air makes the pilot arc unnecessary

questions.stem: Which is a sign that a plasma cutter's nozzle and electrode need changing?
options: The cut is narrower and cleaner than before
The arc wanders and the kerf gets wider and rougher
The air pressure gauge reads much higher than it usually does
The machine's fan runs for longer after cutting

questions.stem: Compared with an arc welding machine, why does a plasma cutter carry a greater risk of electric shock?
options: It sends alternating current at 50 Hz to the torch
Its torch is made of metal with no insulation
It needs water on the work to cool the cut
Its open-circuit voltage is much higher

questions.stem: A trainee in your team is cutting with the cylinders lying on the floor 'because the trolley is in use'. What should you do?
options: Stop the work, stand them upright and secure them
Let him carry on, but keep the flame small
Tell him to roll them closer to the cutting bay
Report it at the end of the week if it happens again

questions.stem: A backfire happened three times on one torch during a job. What should go in your report?
options: Nothing, as backfires are normal and harmless
Only that the job was finished on time
The torch, the nozzle, what happened and what you did
The name of the gas supplier and its phone number

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for the area beside a cut or weld where the heat has changed the metal, but the metal did not melt?
What is the name for the slag and re-solidified metal left stuck to the bottom edge of a cut?
What are the curved lines on a cut face, left by the cutting oxygen stream, called?
What is the name of the shaped copper part at the end of a plasma torch, with a small hole that the arc passes through?
What is the name for the distance between the end of a plasma torch and the plate being cut?
Which flammable gas can build up under the plate, and explode, when aluminium is plasma cut over a water table?
What do the letters SDS stand for, on the sheet that gives the hazards of a gas and how to handle it?
What is the name of the very hard, brittle structure that forms when hot high-carbon steel cools too quickly?
What is the name of the flame that has more oxygen than fuel gas, with a short, sharp inner cone and a harsh hiss?
What is the name for the small uncut parts left on purpose to hold a part in the plate until the last cut?
What do the letters LPG stand for?
A cutting nozzle uses about 50 litres of oxygen a minute. How many litres are used in 30 minutes of cutting?
A part needs four straight cuts, each 450 mm long. What is the total length of cut, in mm?
On a cutting torch, what is the part called that is pressed to release the cutting oxygen?
The oxygen for a job costs J$9 600 and lasts 8 hours of cutting. What is the oxygen cost per hour, in J$?

essays.stem: You are given a drawing of 20 base plates to be cut from one sheet of 10 mm mild steel plate. Explain how you would plan the cutting job: the process, the layout, the allowances, the cut order, the equipment checks and the people you need.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing to confirm the plate thickness, the part sizes, the number of parts and the tolerance. For 10 mm mild steel, oxy-fuel cutting with a straight-edge guide is suitable. I lay out the parts on the plate, nested close together to save material, and allow for the kerf width given in the nozzle chart by cutting on the waste side of each line. I plan the cut order so that the plate stays stiff for as long as possible: cut from the free edge inwards, cut strips first, and leave small tabs where parts might move. I choose the nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart and check that there is enough gas. I check the set, the cutting table and the fire precautions, and write a short risk assessment. I give each member a job: marking out, cutting, cleaning slag, checking sizes and fire watch, and I brief the team. Finally I prepare an inspection sheet so that each part can be checked against the drawing.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing (thickness, sizes, number, tolerance) and chooses the process
Nests the parts and allows for the kerf by cutting on the waste side
Plans the cut order to control distortion (stiff plate, tabs)
Nozzle and pressures from the chart; gas supply, equipment and fire checks; risk assessment
Shares out tasks, briefs the team and prepares an inspection sheet

essays.stem: A customer brings three jobs: cutting 3 mm stainless steel sheet, 8 mm aluminium plate, and 60 mm mild steel. Explain which thermal cutting process you would choose for each, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: For the 3 mm stainless steel sheet I would use plasma cutting. Oxy-fuel cannot cut stainless steel properly, because its chromium oxide melts at a higher temperature than the steel and will not run out of the cut. Plasma melts the metal with a very hot arc and blows it out, giving a narrow cut with little heat and distortion on thin sheet. For the 8 mm aluminium I would also use plasma, for a similar reason: aluminium oxide melts far above the aluminium, and aluminium carries heat away so fast that an oxy-fuel torch would only melt it. (A saw is another choice for straight cuts.) For the 60 mm mild steel I would use oxy-fuel cutting with a large nozzle, as the maker's chart gives. Mild steel burns readily in the oxygen jet and its oxide melts below the steel, so oxy-fuel cuts thick carbon steel cheaply and well, with no power supply. A plasma machine big enough for 60 mm would be very costly. For each job I plan fume control: stainless and aluminium fumes need extraction.
markingPoints: Stainless: plasma, because its chromium oxide melts above the metal
Aluminium: plasma (or a saw), because of its high-melting oxide and fast heat loss
Thick mild steel: oxy-fuel with a large nozzle from the chart, because it burns and its oxide melts low
Notes the cost and thickness limits of plasma
Plans fume and safety controls for each job

essays.stem: Explain how you would inspect a batch of flame-cut parts against the drawing and a cut quality standard, and what you would do with parts that fail.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure the parts are cool and the slag is removed. I measure each part against the drawing with a steel rule or tape and a square, and record the sizes; anything outside the tolerance is marked. I check the cut faces against the cut quality standard the job uses, or against a sample of a good cut: the top edge should be sharp and not melted, the face square to the plate, the drag lines fine and nearly straight, and the bottom edge free of stuck slag. I look for gouges, notches and cracks, especially on high-carbon steel. I record the results for each part on an inspection sheet with the job number, the date and my name. Parts that are too big or rough can be ground or cut again to size. Parts that are too small, cracked or badly gouged are put in a quarantine area with a reject tag, and I report them to the supervisor, who decides whether they are scrapped or used elsewhere. I also look for a pattern in the faults, so that the cause can be put right.
markingPoints: Parts cool and clean; sizes measured against the drawing and tolerance
Cut face checked against the standard or a sample: top edge, squareness, drag lines, slag, gouges, cracks
Results recorded on an inspection sheet
Failed parts reworked if possible; otherwise tagged, quarantined and reported
Looks for the cause of repeated faults

essays.stem: A trainee's cuts in 12 mm plate show (1) a melted, rounded top edge, (2) heavy slag stuck on the bottom, and (3) a hollow (concave) face. Explain the likely cause of each and how you would correct it.
essays.modelAnswer: (1) A melted, rounded top edge usually means the preheat flames are too strong, the nozzle is too close to the plate, or the travel is too slow. I would check the nozzle size and the pressures against the chart, set neutral preheat flames of the right size, keep the inner cones just clear of the plate (about 2–3 mm) and travel a little faster. (2) Heavy slag on the bottom edge usually comes from the wrong travel speed, too little cutting oxygen, or a dirty nozzle. I would check the oxygen pressure, clean or change the nozzle, and find the speed at which the cut sounds steady and the sparks leave the bottom at a slight angle back. (3) A hollow face usually comes from too much cutting oxygen pressure, or a nozzle too big for the plate. I would lower the oxygen pressure to the chart figure or fit the right nozzle. After each change I would watch the trainee make a test cut, compare it with a good sample, and record what was changed.
markingPoints: Rounded top edge: preheat too strong, nozzle too close or travel too slow, with the correction
Bottom slag: wrong speed, low cutting oxygen or dirty nozzle, with the correction
Concave face: too much cutting oxygen or nozzle too big, with the correction
Checks the nozzle and pressures against the maker's chart
Test cut after each change, compared with a sample, and recorded

essays.stem: Explain why and how steel is preheated before cutting or welding, how the temperature is checked, and what can go wrong if the preheat is skipped.
essays.modelAnswer: Preheating means warming the steel before it is cut or welded. Thick steel, high-carbon steel and some alloy steels harden if they cool quickly, because the cold metal around the hot area draws the heat away. A hard edge can crack, and in welding, preheat also helps hydrogen to escape and reduces cracking and distortion. The procedure or drawing gives the preheat temperature. I heat with a heating nozzle or a large flame, moving it evenly over the area and through the thickness, not just the surface, and over a band on each side of the joint or cut line. I check the temperature with temperature-indicating crayons or a contact thermometer, at the distance from the joint that the procedure gives, and I keep it at that temperature while the work is done. If the preheat is skipped, the cut edge or weld may harden and crack, sometimes hours later, and the part may fail in use. Overheating is also wrong, so I check that I do not go above the maximum.
markingPoints: What preheat is, and which steels need it (thick, high-carbon, alloy)
Why: slows cooling, stops hardening and cracking, lets hydrogen escape
How: even heating through the thickness, over a band either side, to the procedure's temperature
Checked with crayons or a contact thermometer at the stated distance, and kept while working
What goes wrong if skipped (cracking, sometimes delayed), and the risk of overheating

essays.stem: A welded steel beam has bent upwards along its length (cambered) after welding. Explain how you would plan and carry out flame straightening, including the heat pattern, temperature control and checking.
essays.modelAnswer: First I measure the camber: I stretch a string line or lay a straight edge along the beam, measure the gap at marked points, and mark the convex (long) side. I check the steel type, because high-strength steels need a written procedure and a lower temperature limit. I support the beam so that it can move, keeping everyone clear. I plan V heats on the web, with the wide end of each V at the convex flange and the point about two-thirds to three-quarters of the way across, and a strip heat across the convex flange in line with each V. I heat with a heating nozzle, starting at the point of the V and working out to the wide end, keeping the steel no hotter than a dull red, checked with temperature crayons, and I let it cool in air. After each heat has cooled, I measure again and record the result, and I add more heats only if needed, spread along the beam. Finally I check the beam against the tolerance on the drawing and record the result.
markingPoints: Measures and marks the camber (string line or straight edge) and checks the steel type
Supports the beam safely; plans V heats on the web, wide end at the convex flange, with strip heats on that flange
Heats from the point of the V outwards, no hotter than dull red, checked with crayons
Lets each heat cool, measures again, records, and adds heats only if needed
Final check against the drawing tolerance, and recorded

essays.stem: You are leading a team that must cut out old steel on a hotel site in Port Antonio. Explain how you would plan and control the hot work safely, from the permit to the fire watch.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work I visit the site with the hotel's person in charge and get a hot work permit. I find out what the steel is, whether it has paint or coatings, and what is around and below the area. I clear or cover anything that can burn for 10 m or more, and I cover gaps, drains and openings so that sparks cannot fall through. I check that suitable fire extinguishers are at hand and that everyone knows the alarm, the exits and how to call for help. I check the gas set and the cylinders, secure them upright, and leak test before lighting. I give the team a safety talk: the PPE, who cuts, who keeps the fire watch, and how to stop the work. During the work I keep guests and staff out with barriers and signs, and I stop work if conditions change. After the work, the fire watch stays for the time the permit sets, often 30–60 minutes, checking the area, below it and behind walls. Then I close the permit with the hotel and record the job.
markingPoints: Hot work permit from the site, and a check of the steel, coatings and surroundings
Combustibles cleared for 10 m or more, drains and gaps covered, extinguishers and emergency plan
Gas set checked, cylinders secured, leak tested; team briefed with roles (cutter, fire watch)
Barriers and signs for guests and staff; work stopped if conditions change
Fire watch after the work for the permit's time; permit closed and the job recorded

essays.stem: Explain how oxygen, acetylene and LPG are held inside their cylinders, how you judge how much gas is left in each, and how you would plan the gas supply for a long cutting job.
essays.modelAnswer: Oxygen is a compressed gas, so the pressure on the contents gauge falls in step with the amount left: a cylinder at half its full pressure is about half full. Acetylene is dissolved in acetone, held in a porous filling, so its pressure changes with the temperature as well as the amount; it is best judged by weighing. It must be stored and used upright, and not drawn off too fast, or acetone comes out with the gas. LPG is stored as a liquid, so its pressure stays about the same until the liquid is nearly used up; the only reliable way to tell how much is left is to weigh the cylinder and take away the empty (tare) weight stamped on it. For a long job I would estimate the gas use from the nozzle chart and the hours of cutting, check the contents of every cylinder before starting, order spare full cylinders in good time, and arrange safe storage, upright and secured, with oxygen kept apart from the fuel gases. I would record the gas used so that the next job can be planned better.
markingPoints: Oxygen: compressed gas, so the gauge shows the contents
Acetylene: dissolved in acetone; judged by weight; kept upright; not drawn off too fast
LPG: liquid, so the pressure stays steady until nearly empty; weigh it and take off the tare
Plans use from the nozzle chart and hours, orders spares, and stores cylinders safely
Records the gas used to plan future jobs

essays.stem: Describe the safe set-up, use and care of a plasma cutter, and explain how you would get the best cut quality from it.
essays.modelAnswer: Before use I read the maker's instructions and check the machine: the mains lead, plug and torch lead are undamaged, the air supply is clean and dry with the filter drained, and the air pressure is set to the maker's figure. I check the consumables (electrode, swirl ring, nozzle and shield) with the power isolated, and replace any that are worn or pitted. I fix the work clamp firmly to clean metal on the job, close to the cut, and set the current for the material and thickness from the maker's chart. I wear a helmet or goggles with a filter shade suited to the current, gloves, flame-resistant clothing and ear protection, and use fume extraction, especially for stainless and coated steel. For a good cut I keep the stand-off distance steady (a guide or a drag shield helps, where the maker allows it), hold the torch square to the plate, and travel at a speed where the sparks come out of the bottom at a slight angle back. Too slow gives dross; too fast and the cut does not go through. After use I switch off, isolate, clean up and report worn parts.
markingPoints: Pre-use checks: leads, torch, and clean, dry air at the right pressure
Consumables checked or changed only with the power isolated
Work clamp on clean metal near the cut; current from the maker's chart
PPE (shade for the current, ear protection) and fume extraction
Cut quality: steady stand-off, torch square, right speed; shut down and report

essays.stem: During cutting, a flashback happens on a trainee's torch. Explain the immediate actions, how you would find the cause, and what your incident report would contain.
essays.modelAnswer: A flashback is when the flame burns back inside the torch or hose, often with a squeal or hiss and a hot handle. At once the trainee closes the torch valves (oxygen first, unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), then the cylinder valves, and moves back. I check that no one is hurt and that nothing is burning, and I tag the set out of use. When it is safe, I look for the cause: a nozzle overheated or blocked with spatter, a nozzle held against the work, wrong pressures, a leaking or loose nozzle seat, hoses not purged before lighting, or faulty check valves. I have the torch, hoses and flashback arrestors checked and replaced as the maker requires, because an arrestor may need replacing after it has stopped a flashback. My incident report gives the date, time and place, the people involved, what happened, the equipment and its serial numbers, the immediate actions, the likely cause, the repairs, and what will be done to stop it happening again, such as retraining on lighting up. I sign it and give it to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Recognises a flashback; torch valves then cylinder valves closed at once, as the maker says
Checks for injury and fire; tags the set out of use
Finds the cause (overheated or blocked nozzle, wrong pressures, no purge, faulty valves)
Torch, hoses and arrestors checked or replaced as the maker requires
Incident report: details, actions, cause, repairs and prevention, signed

practical1.title: Planned oxy-fuel cutting of a nested set of parts from 10 mm plate, with an inspection and gas-use record
practical1.brief: Your group is given a drawing of a set of parts to cut from one piece of 10 mm mild steel plate, about 600 mm × 400 mm: for example four base plates 150 mm × 150 mm, four gussets (right-angled triangles 100 mm × 100 mm) and two strips 50 mm × 400 mm, with a tolerance of ±1.5 mm or as the drawing says. First, as a group, plan the job on paper: a nested layout with the kerf allowed for, the cut order, the nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart, a short risk assessment, and who does each task. One member leads the planning and the check before lighting; another member leads the inspection. Mark out the plate. Every member makes at least two of the cuts, using a straight-edge guide, while another member keeps fire watch. Read the oxygen contents gauge before and after, and estimate the oxygen used. When the parts are cool, chip and grind off the slag, measure every part against the drawing, compare the cut faces with a good sample, and record the results on an inspection sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the plan, inspection sheet, gas record and photos once for the whole group, when the area is clean and the set is shut down.
materials: 10 mm mild steel plate, about 600 mm × 400 mm
Oxy-acetylene (or oxy-propane) cutting set with flashback arrestors and check valves, cutting nozzles, tip cleaners and a spark lighter
Soapstone, scriber, steel rule, tape measure, square and centre punch
Chipping hammer, wire brush and angle grinder
Cutting table with slats, fire extinguisher and fire blanket
The drawing, a planning sheet, an inspection sheet and a gas record

practical2.title: Flame straightening a distorted welded tee and preheating a thick plate to a procedure, with a heating record
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a welded tee made from two pieces of 75 mm × 10 mm flat bar about 600 mm long, which has bowed after welding, and a piece of 20 mm mild steel plate about 300 mm × 150 mm. Part 1: mark points every 100 mm along the tee, measure the bow at each point with a straight edge or string line, and record the readings. As a group, plan the heats (where the V heats or line heats go, how hot, and how the temperature is checked) and write the plan on the heating record. Every member makes at least one heat while a second member checks the temperature with temperature crayons and a third keeps fire watch. Let each heat cool in air, measure again and record the change. Stop when the bow is within the tolerance the assessor sets. Part 2: preheat the 20 mm plate, as if for welding, to the temperature the assessor sets, using a heating nozzle. Heat it evenly, check it with the crayons on both faces at the distance the assessor sets, and record the time taken and the readings. Every member takes a turn at heating or checking. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the heating record and photos once for the whole group.
materials: A welded tee of two 75 mm × 10 mm flat bars, about 600 mm long, bowed from welding (made ready by the assessor)
20 mm mild steel plate, about 300 mm × 150 mm
Oxy-acetylene set with a heating nozzle, flashback arrestors and a spark lighter
Temperature-indicating crayons in the ratings the assessor gives, or a contact thermometer
Straight edge, string line, steel rule and soapstone
Firebricks or heat-proof supports, clamps and tongs

checklist: Measured and recorded the bow accurately at the marked points
Helped plan the heat pattern and can explain why it works
Made at least one heat in the planned place, starting at the point of the V, no hotter than dull red
Checked temperatures with the crayons correctly when it was their turn
Let each heat cool in air before measuring again, and recorded the result
Heated the thick plate evenly and checked it at the set distance on both faces
Kept fire watch or checked temperatures when asked
Wore correct PPE and shut the set down safely
safety: A heating nozzle uses a lot of fuel gas: use the nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart, and do not draw acetylene off faster than the supplier allows
Clear away anything that can burn and keep an extinguisher at hand; keep fire watch during and after the work
Treat all heated parts as hot; use tongs and mark hot work
Wear tinted goggles, leather gloves and flame-resistant clothing
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
